data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms without smuggling in induction, provided the preference is framed as a methodological rule for maximizing 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) and informational content rather than probabilistic confidence. The cost of accepting this defense is the abandonment of the hope that science converges on probable truth, replacing it with a gamble on bold, falsifiable conjectures that may still be false but are closer to the truth than their predecessors.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If Tichý and Miller's proof that Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude is logically incoherent for false theories holds universally, then the mechanism collapses as there is no coherent metric to prefer one false theory over another.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the preference for better-corroborated theories implicitly assumes that the future will resemble the past (uniformity of nature) to justify acting on them, then induction has been smuggled back in despite verbal denials.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If scientists actually act on high-probability low-content theories in critical applications (e.g., bridge building) rather than bold high-content theories, the descriptive claim that they prefer corroboration is false.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "The argument proceeds by distinguishing between 'probability' (logical likelihood based on past frequency) and 'verisimilitude' (ontological proximity to truth). Popper's rejection of induction targets the former; his preference for corroboration targets the latter. By treating corroboration as a report of a theory's survival under severe tests (which increases its empirical content), scientists select theories with higher potential verisimilitude. This selection is not an inductive inference that the theory *will* hold in the future, but a rational choice to act on the hypothesis that has survived the most rigorous attempts at falsification, thereby offering the greatest leverage for further discovery. The 'smuggling' charge fails because the preference relies on the logical asymmetry of falsification (one counter-example destroys, many supports do not prove) rather than a symmetry of confirmation.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": []}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
